project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The lignin leaves the mill as wet cake and no lignin dryer is available, so dry-powder applications would require buyer-side or new drying capacity.
Solvent or membrane fractionation is not available, limiting applications that require fractionated lignin unless new equipment is added.
Chemical modification equipment is not available, limiting modified-lignin applications unless processing is outsourced or installed.
The stream is currently routed to internal fuel, so an external-value pathway would need to replace or account for that use.
Moisture is uncertain and affects dry tonnage and shipping mass; moisture control and logistics must therefore be confirmed before commercialization.
Covered cake storage is finite, so inventory and dispatch planning must account for the available storage capacity.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, preventing comparison with requirements that depend on these properties.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional demonstration data, not measurements from a real mill; all figures must be replaced with mill production records and laboratory data before decisions are made.
The reported lignin content uses a method stated for illustration only; confirm the analytical method before comparing it with buyer specifications.
Moisture is identified as uncertain and should be measured over time because it determines dry tonnage and shipped mass.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are not measured.
The deterministic validation passed the dry-matter balance, composition check, and missing-data-gap check.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-03#3: With phenol at around 1,000 USD per tonne, substituting part of the phenol in PF resins with lignin is estimated to add about 800 USD per marginal tonne of pulp (not per tonne of lignin); the additional operating costs are not known.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can replace part of phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used for plywood and other wood-based-panel adhesives.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin for veneer plywood is reported as industrially proven and capable of meeting Bonding Class 3.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include plywood producers and manufacturers of wood-based panels that use phenol-formaldehyde adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The principal incumbent material is phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resin.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resin.
The plywood resin application is associated with EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3, and the cited study evaluated viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard.

limitations: The evidence combines review literature, vendor technical literature, and a laboratory plywood study.
The reported TRL 8 applies to biobased phenolic resins generally, not specifically to kraft-lignin resin.
The UPM performance and cost claims are manufacturer claims without a cited test report.
The cited depolymerized-lignin molecular-weight range is not established as a requirement for Pinecrest's delivered cake.
missing_information: No named buyers, purchase commitments, contract terms, or regional demand split is provided.
No current lignin price, delivered resin price, market volume applicable to the target region, or offtake volume is provided.
Pinecrest cake's molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, ash, and moisture suitability are not established for this application.
The evidence does not quantify the drying, activation, or depolymerization cost for Pinecrest material.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents an established producer's industrially proven lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin and a plywood qualification claim, which is stronger than research-only interest. However, it does not document several producers selling to established buyers.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can serve as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyols in rigid polyurethane or polyisocyanurate insulation foam.
Kraft lignin has also been studied as a partial polyol replacement in flexible polyurethane foam, with the evidence suggesting possible fit for heavy-duty foams rather than automotive flexible foam.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include rigid insulation-foam manufacturers using polyurethane or polyisocyanurate systems.
Potential customers also include flexible-foam manufacturers, particularly those serving heavy-duty foam applications.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: A cited rigid-foam criterion is total lignin hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, equivalent in the source to 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl groups.
Rigid PUR/PIR foam must be evaluated against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications in the cited study, including compressive strength and closed-cell content.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction to reach target polyurethane properties.

limitations: Most evidence is from laboratory foam studies, and the studies report variable performance among lignins.
The cited polyurethane TRL 6 covers a broad row of uses rather than kraft-lignin foam specifically.
The flexible-foam study compared results with automotive OEM requirements but did not establish commercial automotive qualification.
A review indicates that commercialization remains constrained by consistency, technical performance, and production cost.
missing_information: No named polyurethane buyer, commercial offtake, purchase specification, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No current price comparison between Pinecrest lignin and petroleum polyol is provided.
Pinecrest's total hydroxyl value, composition, moisture, viscosity behavior, and compatibility with polyurethane formulations are not established.
The mill lacks chemical-modification equipment, and the evidence does not provide the cost or availability of outsourced modification.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows substantial research activity and a broad market context, but it does not document a commercial lignin-polyurethane sale, buyer, or development partnership; it also explicitly describes commercialization as limited.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

applications.statement: Lignin can be used as a precursor for carbon fiber, although the evidence identifies demanding purification, spinning, and precursor-quality requirements.

Kraft lignin can be converted into hard carbon for sodium-ion battery anodes; a review reports higher initial coulombic efficiency for hard carbon made from kraft lignin than from sulfonated lignin under the cited conditions.
Lignin can also be converted into activated carbon, including material made from lignin that is too impure for other carbon applications.

target_customers.statement: Potential carbon-fiber customers include carbon-fiber manufacturers with melt-spinning and carbon-fiber production capability.
Potential hard-carbon customers include battery manufacturers and carmakers that qualify lignin-based anode materials.
Potential activated-carbon customers include producers of activated carbon products.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based carbon fiber is an incumbent or competing carbon-fiber material.
Anthracite is a fossil-derived competing precursor for sodium-ion battery hard carbon.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber required purification, and softwood lignin requires a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning.
Battery-material qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years according to the cited company material.
Activated carbon has no strict precursor-quality limitation in the cited study, although lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion.

limitations: The carbon-materials pathway combines three products with materially different specifications, so pathway-level evidence is heterogeneous.
Carbon-fiber specifications are cited secondhand and the underlying study used lignin from a near-neutral hemicellulose extraction process rather than standard kraft pulping.
The carbon-fiber development results include older work and a modelled, rather than measured, cost estimate.
The hard-carbon evidence is a review, while the battery qualification and pilot evidence comes from company material with forward-looking statements.
Activated-carbon evidence is from a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation.
missing_information: No named buyer, purchase commitment, contract, or regional demand volume is provided for Pinecrest lignin.
No evidence establishes that Pinecrest cake meets the carbon-fiber precursor specifications or battery-anode performance requirements.
No process, drying, purification, carbonization, activation, or logistics cost is provided for Pinecrest material.
The evidence does not provide a commercial qualification result for Pinecrest lignin or a current status update for the cited battery-material scale-up plans.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents an industrially relevant precursor-fiber pilot and battery-manufacturer/carmaker qualification activity, which supports a development-stage market signal. It does not document commercial sales by multiple producers to established buyers.

processing_requirements.statement: Pinecrest lignin would need activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
The wet cake would need drying or a buyer-side drying solution because no lignin dryer is available at the mill.
Qualification should address viscosity, bonding strength, free formaldehyde, and the cited EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 application.

technical_maturity.statement: Biobased phenolic-resin production is reported at TRL 8, indicating a mature technology base, although Pinecrest-specific qualification remains necessary.

adoption_barriers.statement: Plywood and wood-panel customers would need to qualify Pinecrest lignin against incumbent phenol-based resin systems and relevant bonding performance.
The mill has no chemical-modification equipment, so activation or depolymerization would require new equipment or an external processing partner.
No named buyers, purchase commitments, contract terms, regional demand split, current prices, or offtake volume are available.

ranking_changers: Completion of phenolic-resin feedstock compatibility and economics could move phenolic resins from insufficient data to the leading ranked pathway, given its assessed technical-readiness score of 5, market-evidence score of 4, and feasibility score of 3.

report.summary: Carbon materials is the current ranked first pathway at attractiveness 2.19, but it is not a definitive commercial recommendation. documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.

With phenol at around 1,000 USD per tonne, substituting part of the phenol in PF resins with lignin is estimated to add about 800 USD per marginal tonne of pulp (not per tonne of lignin); the additional operating costs are not known.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
